paper.title: A multi-paradigm and longitudinal EEG dataset including the “sixth-finger” and “affected-hand” motor imagery of stroke patients
paper.article_license: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (article; do not infer dataset license)

claims.name: cohort
claims.quote: This study recruited a total of 24 stroke patients from Tianjin Huanhu Hospital, including 18 males and 6 females. The patients ranged in age from 34 to 77 years, with a mean age of 55.75 years. Among them, 15 had right hemiplegia and 9 had left hemiplegia. And fourteen patients received brain-computer interface (BCI) training (BCI group), while 10 patients received conventional physical rehabilitation therapy (Traditional group). The BCI training involved a 2-week rehabilitation program using the brain-controlled “sixth-finger”15,17 system independently developed by the research team from Tianjin University. The conventional physical training consisted of a 2-week rehabilitation program and administered by rehabilitation physicians from Tianjin Huanhu Hospital. The BCI group and traditional group received equivalent training dosages. Each intervention consisted of 8 training sessions over 2 weeks, with 4 sessions per week, and each session lasted approximately 45 min. In addition, all patients underwent three functional assessments: immediately before the intervention (pre-training), immediately after the intervention (post-training), and 1 month after the intervention (follow-up).

claims.name: missing_followup_ids
claims.quote: When using this dataset, it is important to consider the following: Due to individual patient circumstances, not all participants completed every experimental task. Specifically, subjects sub-05, sub-17, sub-18, sub-20 and sub-21 lack data from the follow-up sessions. Additionally, as this dataset includes patient data from multiple groups, appropriate adjustments to the code and data folder organization should be made when analyzing EEG data across different groups. To ensure de-identification of the raw data, all participant identifiers were replaced with sequential ID codes. Furthermore, any fields in the data files that could potentially contain identifiable information, including acquisition-site information, recording dates and names, were removed.

claims.name: trial_total_reported
claims.quote: This study collected neurorehabilitation data from 24 stroke patients, including EEG recordings under three assessment time points (pre-training, post-training, and follow-up period), two motor imagery paradigms (SF-MI and AH-MI), and resting state. A total of 5,360 MI trials and 5,360 resting-state trials were acquired. The public dataset comprises three elements: raw EEG data, preprocessed data, and patient information. The preprocessed data can be used directly with the provided code to visualize results and conduct classification tasks. Researchers are also encouraged to repurpose the dataset for other investigations. To our knowledge, this constitutes the first large-scale MI dataset for stroke patients that combines multi-paradigm, including the “sixth-finger” and “affected-hand” MI, with longitudinal-training.

claims.name: protocol_and_events

value.tasks: Affected-hand grasp imagery or robotic sixth-finger grasp imagery

claims.quote: The data collection paradigm was consistent across all collection phases, as shown in Fig. 1(A). Each trial lasted 14 s and was initiated by pressing the space bar. A green fixation cross was first displayed at the center of the screen for 7 s, during which the patients remained in a resting state. This was followed by a gray circle presented for 1 second to prompt the patients to prepare for the MI task. Subsequently, MI period commenced for 6 s, during which a picture cue randomly appeared on the screen—either showing a clenched fist of the affected hand or a flexed “sixth-finger”—to indicate the type of AH-MI or SF-MI task in this trial. Therefore, this dataset comprises EEG signals from three paradigms: the rest task (events as Label 1), AH-MI task (events as Label 2), and SF-MI task (events as Label 3):Fig. 1Experimental scenarios and paradigm. (A) Experimental paradigm. (B) Experimental scene. (C) Electrode positions.

claims.name: acquisition
claims.quote: EEG signals were recorded using a 64-channel NeuSen W system (Neuracle) with Ag/AgCl electrodes arranged according to the international 10–20 system. The reference and ground electrodes were placed at CPz and the forehead, respectively. Signals were sampled at 250 Hz and a 50 Hz notch filter was applied to suppress line noise.

claims.name: preprocessing
claims.quote: Preprocessing was performed in EEGLAB. The steps included: (1) band-pass filtering between 5~35 Hz and application of a 50 Hz notch filter; (2) re-referencing to the common average reference (CAR); (3) removal of peripheral channels prone to motion artifacts, resulting in 40 channels for analysis shown in Fig. 1(C); (4) manual artifact rejection to identify and remove transient artifacts characterized by abnormal amplitude fluctuations at specific time points, with channels exhibiting persistent abnormal amplitude patterns interpolated; and (5) independent component analysis (ICA) to identify and remove components associated with eye-movement artifacts, based on scalp topographies, temporal waveforms.

claims.name: dataset_structure
claims.quote: Our dataset is available in the Figshare repository21, is organized as Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS)22, a widely adopted format for open EEG datasets, facilitating straightforward access and reuse. The dataset structure is illustrated in Fig. 2. The repository is divided into four main sections: (1) Raw data, containing the original EEG recordings for each subject throughout the entire experiment, stored as ‘.set/.fdt’ files; (2) Preprocessed data, stored as ‘.mat’ files; (3) Additional information, including patient details, electrode locations, and EEG event markers; and (4) Code, provided as MATLAB scripts.Fig. 2The EEG dataset structure.

claims.name: paper_classification

value.validation: 10-fold random per-subject partition; mean across subjects

claims.quote: In this study, each trial of the SF-MI and AH-MI tasks lasted 6 s. Based on the earlier finding that the ERD phenomenon tends to stabilize after 0.5~1 s, the EEG data segment from 1 s~5 s after the onset of the MI task was selected for classification. The extracted 4 s data segment from each trial was treated as an independent sample, thereby ensuring trial-level independence and preventing overly optimistic classification performance caused by temporal adjacency between samples. And other researchers may adopt customized sample-segmentation strategies according to their specific research objectives and analytical requirements. To demonstrate the inherent classifiability induced by the MI paradigm itself, this study employed classical machine learning algorithms for the binary classification task between SF-MI and AH-MI. EEG features were extracted using the Common Spatial Pattern (CSP) method, and the resulting feature vectors were subsequently classified using both support vector machine (SVM) and linear discriminant analysis (LDA) classifiers. A 10-fold cross-validation procedure was applied, in which the EEG data of each subject was randomly partitioned into 10 groups. For each fold, one group was used as the test set and the remaining nine groups as the training set. This process was repeated 10 times, and the average of the results was taken as the classification accuracy for each subject. The final classification accuracy was then computed as the mean across all subjects.

claims.name: code_availability
claims.quote: Code availabilityAll MATLAB scripts used in this study for preprocessing, feature extraction, plotting, and classification are available in the ‘code’ folder21. These scripts require users to install the EEGLAB toolbox in advance. The subject details, electrodes information, and event markers along with raw datasets and preprocessed datasets, have been made publicly available21.

limits: Paper identifies raw EEG as continuous unsegmented .set/.fdt but actual release binary/file-pair validity is outside this paper-only check.
Paper reports 5,360 total MI trials and 5,360 resting-state trials; per-run counts and per-class balance are not stated in narrative text and are not inferred.
Assessment EEG across pre/post/follow-up with 2-week intervention does not by itself document adaptive decoder update logs or establish causal human skill retention.
